title: Steam, Electric or Gasoline? The Great Race of 1900
summary: Around 1900, nobody knew what kind of engine cars would use. Some cars hummed quietly on batteries, some hissed with steam, and some banged and smoked with gasoline. One electric car even became the first to zoom faster than 100 km/h!

sections.heading: Three Kinds of Car on One Street
paragraphs: Imagine standing on a busy street in New York City in the year 1900. Horses still clop past pulling wagons and cabs, but every now and then something strange rolls by with no horse at all. First comes a cab that makes almost no sound, just a soft whirr and the crunch of its wheels. A few minutes later a little buggy glides past with a faint hiss and a puff of white vapour, like a kettle on wheels. Then a third machine comes rattling around the corner, popping and banging, leaving a blue cloud of smelly smoke behind it. People cover their noses. A horse shies away.

Those three machines were the three teams in one of the most important contests in the history of technology. The first was an electric car, running on batteries. The second was a steam car, which burned fuel to boil water. The third was a gasoline car, with the new internal combustion engine you met in Parts 3 to 6. In 1900 nobody knew which one would win. Many sensible people would have bet against the noisy gasoline car.

In fact, around 1900 gasoline cars were a minority on American roads. Only a few thousand cars were built in the United States that year, and steam and electric cars together made up most of them. Sources disagree on the exact numbers. One often-quoted estimate says roughly 40 percent of American cars were steam, about 38 percent electric and only about 22 percent gasoline; the US Department of Energy says that electric cars alone were roughly a third of the vehicles on the road. Whichever count you use, the picture is the same: the gasoline car was the underdog.

So how did the underdog win? To find out, we need to meet the teams, their inventors and their heroes, and look at what each kind of car was good at and bad at. Along the way we will see the first car ever to break 100 kilometres per hour, a steam car that flew through the air on a Florida beach, and a clever starter motor that changed everything.

sections.heading: Team Electric: Batteries on Wheels
paragraphs: Electric cars are often talked about as something brand new, but they are actually older than most gasoline cars. The key ingredient was the rechargeable battery. In 1859 the French scientist Gaston Planté invented the lead-acid battery, a box of lead plates in acid that could be charged up with electricity, then give that electricity back later. It is the same basic type of battery that still starts most gasoline cars today. Better versions appeared around 1881, and suddenly inventors had a way to carry stored electricity around.

One of the first to try was Gustave Trouvé, a brilliant Parisian electrical engineer who invented dozens of gadgets, from a tool for finding bullets inside wounded soldiers to an early electric outboard motor for boats. In 1881 he took a tricycle made by the English bicycle maker James Starley, fitted it with a small electric motor that he had improved from a Siemens design, and added rechargeable batteries. On 19 April 1881 he rode it along the Rue de Valois in the middle of Paris. It was one of the first electric vehicles ever to carry a person on a city street. Trouvé never managed to patent it, which is one reason his name is not as famous as it deserves to be.

Across the Channel in England, the engineer Thomas Parker was also busy. Parker worked in Wolverhampton, in the industrial Midlands, and he helped bring electric power and trams to British towns. He is reported to have built an electric car around 1884, although the earliest surviving photograph of one of his vehicles dates from 1895. His company, Elwell-Parker, built early electric carriages in the 1890s.

In the United States, a chemist named William Morrison of Des Moines, Iowa, built an electric carriage around 1890 that could carry six people at about 14 miles per hour (roughly 23 km/h). It was really an ordinary wagon with a motor and a heavy load of batteries, but crowds came to see it, and it got Americans excited about horseless carriages.

Then came the first electric taxis. Two engineers in Philadelphia, Henry Morris and Pedro Salom, built electric carriages they called Electrobats. In 1897 their company began running a fleet of electric cabs in New York City, starting with about a dozen and growing to more than 60. The business was soon taken over by the Electric Vehicle Company, which tried to build hundreds more. It even set up stations where a cab's heavy, nearly empty battery could be swapped for a fully charged one, a clever idea that some electric car companies are still experimenting with today. That same year, 1897, London got its own electric cabs designed by Walter Bersey. Londoners nicknamed them Hummingbirds because of the humming noise they made.

sections.heading: The Never Satisfied: Breaking 100 km/h
paragraphs: Now for the most thrilling chapter in Team Electric's story. In 1899, the fastest car in the world was not a gasoline car at all. It was an electric car shaped like a bullet, and its name was La Jamais Contente, which is French for 'The Never Satisfied'.

Its driver was Camille Jenatzy, a Belgian engineer born in 1868 in Schaerbeek, near Brussels. Jenatzy built electric vehicles, and he had a bushy red beard that earned him the nickname 'Le Diable Rouge', the Red Devil. He also had a rival: a French nobleman named Count Gaston de Chasseloup-Laubat, who drove an electric car made by the Jeantaud company. Their contest was one of the first speed duels in motoring history.

The battleground was a straight road at Achères, a small town just west of Paris. On 17 January 1899 Jenatzy covered a timed kilometre at about 66.7 km/h, a new record. The very same day Chasseloup-Laubat went faster. Ten days later Jenatzy came back and reached about 80 km/h. Chasseloup-Laubat answered again, this time with a car given a simple pointed nose to help it slip through the air. Back and forth the record went, like a tennis rally.

Jenatzy decided to end the argument with a car built for nothing but speed. La Jamais Contente was long and narrow, with a body shaped like a torpedo or a cigar. The body was made of partinium, a light alloy containing aluminium, tungsten and magnesium. Underneath were two electric motors, each one driving the rear wheels by chain, and a heavy load of batteries. Together the motors could produce around 68 horsepower for a short burst, an enormous amount for 1899, when Karl Benz's first car had produced less than one. The whole machine weighed about 1,450 kilograms, much of it batteries. It rolled on air-filled Michelin tyres.

The design was not perfect. The driver sat high up, with his head, shoulders and chest sticking out above the smooth body, which spoiled some of the streamlining. The wheels and the chassis underneath were exposed to the wind too. But it was the first car ever built specially to break the land speed record.

On 29 April 1899 (some sources say 1 May), Jenatzy climbed aboard at Achères and switched on the power. The car hummed down the road, faster and faster, and the timekeepers clicked their watches. The result: about 105.9 kilometres per hour, or 65.8 miles per hour. For the first time in history, a car had gone faster than 100 km/h. A person on that road was moving faster than a galloping racehorse and faster than many trains of the day.

La Jamais Contente held the record for about three years, until 1902, when the Frenchman Léon Serpollet beat it in a steam car. Jenatzy himself went on to race gasoline cars and won the important Gordon Bennett Cup race in Ireland in 1903 driving a Mercedes. The bullet-shaped electric car still survives. You can see it today at the National Car and Tourism Museum in the Château de Compiègne, north of Paris.

sections.heading: Team Steam: Kettles That Could Fly
paragraphs: If you think a steam car must have been slow and clumsy, like Cugnot's great wagon in Part 2, the Stanley twins would like a word with you. Francis Edgar Stanley and Freelan Oscar Stanley were identical twins born in 1849 in Kingfield, Maine. They looked so alike that people often could not tell them apart. Before cars, they made a fortune with photographic plates, and they sold that business to the Eastman Kodak company. With the money, they turned to building steam cars.

Their first car ran in 1897. Within a couple of years they had sold more than 200 cars, which made them one of the biggest carmakers in America at the time. In 1902 they founded the Stanley Motor Carriage Company, with its factory in Watertown, Massachusetts. Their cars became known everywhere as Stanley Steamers.

Here is how a Stanley worked, in simple terms. Under the seat sat a round boiler, a strong metal drum full of water threaded with many small tubes. Beneath it was a burner that burned gasoline, or later kerosene, a bit like a giant camping stove. The flames heated the water, the water turned to high-pressure steam, and the steam pushed the pistons of a small two-cylinder engine connected directly to the rear axle. To make the boiler strong, the Stanleys wound piano wire around its outer shell. There was no gearbox at all. The more steam you let in, the faster you went, smoothly and almost silently.

And they could go fast. In January 1906 a Stanley racing car, a low, upturned-canoe-shaped machine nicknamed the Rocket, came to the hard, flat sand of Ormond-Daytona Beach in Florida. Its driver was Fred Marriott, a mechanic from the Stanley factory. According to the company's story, he got the job partly because he was the only bachelor in the team, so if something went wrong there would be no widow left behind. Marriott raced over a measured mile in about 28.2 seconds. That works out to about 127 miles per hour, or roughly 205 km/h. It was the fastest any car had ever gone, and it was several years before any car of any kind went faster.

The next year, 1907, Marriott tried to go even faster in an improved Rocket. The car hit a bump in the sand at an estimated 140 to 150 miles per hour, lifted into the air like a plane taking off, and broke apart when it landed. Marriott was badly hurt but survived. He never tried for the record again, and the Stanleys decided not to risk any more racing.

Marriott's steam car record turned out to be amazingly tough. It stood for more than a hundred years. Only in August 2009 did a British team beat it, at Edwards Air Force Base in California, with a modern steam car called Inspiration. Driver Charles Burnett III averaged about 139.8 miles per hour over a measured mile, and a day later Don Wales pushed the car to about 148 miles per hour over a kilometre.

The Stanleys were not alone. The White company of Cleveland, Ohio, a firm that also made sewing machines, built thousands of steam cars between 1900 and 1911. Rollin White designed a clever boiler made of stacked coils of tube that made steam quickly. White steam cars were tough and comfortable, and one was even used by the US Secret Service, driving along behind President Theodore Roosevelt's horse-drawn carriage. When President William Howard Taft turned the White House stables into a garage in 1909, White cars were among the first vehicles kept there.

sections.heading: Report Cards for Three Racers
paragraphs: If you were buying a car in 1900, which would you have chosen? Let us give each team a report card.

Electric cars scored top marks for being quiet, clean and easy. There was no smoke, no smell and no hot, dangerous fire anywhere. You did not have to change gears or wrestle with a crank. You simply flicked a switch, moved a lever, and off you went. That made them popular with doctors making house calls in town, with city families, and especially with wealthy women, who were the target of many electric car advertisements. Clara Ford, the wife of Henry Ford himself, drove an electric car made by the Detroit Electric company rather than one of her husband's gasoline cars. But electrics had serious weaknesses. Their heavy lead-acid batteries stored only a small amount of energy for their weight. A typical electric car of the time could manage only about 30 to 40 miles (50 to 65 km) before it needed recharging, and its top speed was often only about 15 to 20 miles per hour. Recharging took hours, and outside big cities hardly any homes had electricity at all. The inventor Thomas Edison worked for years on a better nickel-iron battery to fix these problems, but even his improved battery could not close the gap.

Steam cars got high marks for power and smoothness. They could climb steep hills, glide along without changing gear, and, as Fred Marriott showed, go astonishingly fast. Their weak points were time and water. On early steam cars, getting the boiler hot enough could take many minutes before you could set off, which was annoying if you just wanted to pop to the shops. They also gulped water, so drivers had to stop to refill often, and in freezing winters the water could freeze. Lighting a burner and watching the pressure gauges took skill. Many people also feared that a boiler might explode, even though Stanley boilers were very strongly made.

Gasoline cars had the worst manners of the three. Their engines were noisy, rattly and smelly. They had to be started with a hand crank, a metal handle stuck into the front of the engine that you had to spin hard with your arm. If the engine fired at the wrong moment, the crank could kick back violently, and broken wrists and arms were common. Changing gear on early gasoline cars was tricky, with grinding and crunching if you got it wrong. But gasoline had one gigantic advantage: it packs an enormous amount of energy into a small, light tank. A gasoline car could travel far, then fill up again in a few minutes from a can. On a long trip into the countryside, that mattered more than anything else.

So in 1900 the race looked close. Electric was best in town, steam was the speed king, and gasoline was best for long journeys. The winner would depend on what changed next: fuel prices, roads, factory methods and one very clever invention.

sections.heading: Why Not Both? Porsche's Early Hybrid
paragraphs: Some inventors asked a different question: why choose? A young Austrian engineer named Ferdinand Porsche, who would later become very famous (and whose story continues in Part 12), came up with a remarkable answer around 1900.

Porsche was working for Jacob Lohner and Company, a Vienna firm that built fine horse-drawn carriages for royalty and the rich. Together they created the Lohner-Porsche. Instead of one big motor connected to the wheels by chains or shafts, Porsche put an electric motor right inside the hub of each front wheel. Each motor turned its own wheel directly, with no gears or chains in between, so very little energy was wasted. These are called hub motors, and the idea is still used in some electric vehicles today. One battery-powered Lohner-Porsche was shown at the great Paris Exposition of 1900, where millions of visitors came to see the newest wonders of science.

The problem, as always, was the battery. One special version, a coach with motors in all four wheels built for a British customer, needed about 1.8 tonnes of batteries. So Porsche tried something cleverer. In his 'Mixte' cars, a gasoline engine did not drive the wheels at all. Instead it turned a generator, which made electricity, which then powered the motors in the wheels. A battery could store extra energy too. A car with both a fuel engine and an electric motor is called a hybrid, and Porsche's Mixte is one of the earliest examples in the world. It also had four-wheel drive in some versions, decades before that became common.

Lohner-Porsche cars were expensive and heavy, and only a few hundred were sold in total. But the idea did not die. Almost a hundred years later, in 1997, Toyota began selling the Prius hybrid in Japan, using a computer-controlled version of the same basic idea, as you will see in Part 18.

sections.heading: How the Race Was Won
paragraphs: Between about 1900 and 1915, the contest swung decisively toward gasoline. No single event did it. Instead, four big changes piled up, each one adding weight on the gasoline side of the scale.

The first change gushed out of the ground in Texas. On 10 January 1901, workers drilling on a low hill called Spindletop, near the town of Beaumont, heard a rumble. Suddenly mud, then gas, then oil came roaring out of the hole and shot more than 150 feet (about 45 metres) into the air. The Lucas gusher, as it was called, sprayed an estimated 100,000 barrels of oil a day, and it took workers nine days to bring it under control. Spindletop was just the start. Huge new oil fields were found in Texas, Oklahoma and California, and the United States became the world's leading oil producer. Gasoline, which had once been an almost useless leftover from making lamp oil, became cheap and plentiful.

The second change was roads. As more people bought cars, they wanted to drive between towns, not just around them. Roads between cities slowly improved, and drivers wanted cars that could go 100 miles or more without stopping for hours. An electric car could not do that, and there were no charging points in the countryside. A gasoline car could, and soon there were places to buy fuel in almost every town. Long range was the gasoline car's superpower.

The third change was price. In 1908 Henry Ford launched the Model T, and his factories found ways to build it faster and cheaper every year (you will see how in Part 11). According to the US Department of Energy, by 1912 a gasoline car could cost about 650 dollars, while an electric roadster cost about 1,750 dollars, almost three times as much. For most families, the choice was easy.

The fourth change solved the gasoline car's worst problem: the dangerous hand crank. A famous story says that in 1910 a car builder named Byron Carter stopped to help a woman whose car had stalled, and the crank kicked back and smashed his jaw, leading to his death. Historians are not sure the story is true in every detail, but it is often told as the reason the boss of Cadillac, Henry Leland, decided cranking had to go. Leland turned to Charles Kettering, an inventive engineer from Ohio whose company was called Delco, short for Dayton Engineering Laboratories Company.

Kettering's solution was brilliant. He fitted the car with a battery and a small but very powerful electric motor. When the driver pressed a button or pedal, the battery sent a strong burst of current to the motor, and the motor turned the engine over through gears until it fired and started running on its own. Then the clever part: once the engine was running, it turned a generator that recharged the battery, ready for the next start. The same electrical system also powered the spark for the engine and the car's electric lights. Electric lights were a big improvement in themselves, since many early cars used gas or oil lamps.

Kettering had a working model by February 1911, and Cadillac put his electric self-starter on its 1912 cars, ordering 12,000 of them. The invention won Cadillac a famous British engineering award, the Dewar Trophy, in 1913. Other carmakers quickly copied the idea. Now anyone could start a gasoline car with the press of a button, without any risk of a broken arm. One of the electric car's biggest selling points, its easy starting, had disappeared overnight.

sections.heading: The Winner Takes the Road
paragraphs: Team Electric and Team Steam did not vanish at once. Electric car sales in the United States peaked in the early 1910s, and more than 300 different American companies built electric vehicles at one time or another. Electric delivery vans, milk floats and factory trucks carried on working for decades, especially in Britain, where battery-powered milk floats hummed through the streets in the early morning until quite recently. But as private cars, electrics slowly faded, and by the 1930s they had nearly disappeared.

Steam cars faded too. White built its last steam car in January 1911 and switched to gasoline cars and trucks. The Stanley company carried on making steam cars, but after Francis Stanley died in a road accident in 1918 the business lost its way, and it closed in 1924. Altogether the Stanleys built about 11,000 steam cars. A few enthusiasts, such as the Doble company in California in the 1920s, built astonishingly advanced steam cars that could start in under a minute, but they were far too expensive for ordinary buyers.

By about 1915, the gasoline car had clearly won the great race. It was not the quietest, the cleanest or, at first, the fastest. It won because it could go far on cheap fuel, because factories learned to build it cheaply, and because clever engineers fixed its worst faults one by one. That is an important lesson about inventions: the winner is not always the one that looks best on day one, but the one that gets improved the fastest.

There is a twist in this tale, of course. A hundred years later, worries about pollution and climate would bring electric cars roaring back, as you will discover in Part 18. But for most of the twentieth century, the road belonged to the gasoline engine. So what exactly was going on inside that noisy metal box under the hood? Let us lift the hood, peer inside, and find out exactly how tiny explosions make a car move.

deepDive: Why did gasoline beat batteries in the early 1900s, and why are batteries winning now? Much of the answer lies in a number engineers call energy density: how much energy a fuel or battery stores per kilogram. Gasoline holds roughly 12 to 13 kilowatt-hours of chemical energy per kilogram. The lead-acid batteries of 1900 stored only a few tens of watt-hours per kilogram, hundreds of times less. Even allowing for the fact that an electric motor turns most of its energy into motion while an early gasoline engine wasted the large majority of its fuel as heat, a gasoline car could carry many times more useful energy for the same weight. That is why electric cars of the era were limited to roughly 30 to 40 miles of range and a top speed of 15 to 20 mph, while gasoline cars could cross whole states. Refuelling also mattered: pouring liquid fuel transfers energy far faster than recharging a battery from a weak early electricity supply, and in 1910 most rural American homes had no electricity at all. Historians also argue about how much the result was decided by technology and how much by business and timing. The Electric Vehicle Company, which ran New York's electric cabs, collapsed partly through poor management and scandals over vehicle performance, not just battery physics. Cheap Texas oil after Spindletop in 1901, Ford's falling prices and the self-starter of 1912 all arrived within about a decade, creating a snowball effect: more gasoline cars led to more filling stations and repair shops, which made gasoline cars even more convenient. Economists call this kind of self-reinforcing advantage a network effect or lock-in. Steam's decline is a similar story. Stanley cars were technically impressive, but the company built only about 11,000 in nearly three decades, while Ford was soon building that many in days. Statistics from this period are uncertain: production and registration figures for 1900 vary from source to source, so the often-quoted split of about 40 percent steam, 38 percent electric and 22 percent gasoline should be treated as a rough estimate rather than a precise count.
funFact: The first car to travel faster than 100 km/h, La Jamais Contente in 1899, was an electric car, not a gasoline one.
